extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, municipal and federal officials, students and scholars of political economy and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and concrete policy standards for integrating large corporate and public-service enterprises into a national democratic economic system, including when to regulate, tax, lease, partially appropriate, or nationalize. Focuses on railroads, municipal franchises, semi-monopolies, and wealth redistribution measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public ownership justified when corporate interest is hostile to public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Public ownership can be justified when the interest of corporations has become "in any essential respect hostile to the public interest," in which case "a constructive industrial policy demands... a much more complete, shifting of the responsibility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats hostility to public interest as a threshold for moving beyond mere regulation to public ownership; this is presented as a clear-cut ground for national action rather than piecemeal fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation must address structural causes, not merely eradicate abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments in corporate "regulation" that merely eradicate abuses attempt to evade a fundamental responsibility by meeting a superficial one and will not restore the old harmony between public and private interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid remedies that only supervise abuses; policy should confront the legal uses of the existing economic system and the deeper problem of distribution of wealth. Overreliance on incessant official interference is criticized as shirking the ultimate problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve managerial efficiency while promoting broader distribution of benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: A national economic policy should preserve the advantages of corporate organization (opportunities for capable managers, efficient operation) while simultaneously seeking better distribution of the fruits of that efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should avoid measures (e.g., certain commission tutelage) that deprive capable managers of opportunities; seek arrangements that retain efficiency but diffuse benefits over a larger social area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graduated taxation of net profits to curb excessive monopoly profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The state can constitute a system of taxation for semi-monopolistic corporations which would deprive them of excessively large margins between cost of production and price — by taxing net profits at a rate graduated to the percentage paid, increasing until it might reach one-half or three-quarters, with limits suggested (not larger than three-quarters except in extreme cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduation must be set so as not to remove incentives for improvement: a properly graduated scale avoids preventing desirable improvements. The proposal is framed as a practical, transitional tool rather than a final formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer automatic regulated recognition over incessant interference
rubrics_metrics.description: An "automatically regulated recognition" of semi-monopolistic corporations is preferable to incessant official interference in management; such transitional recognition can encourage efficiency while preventing dangerous inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is offered as mitigating the harms of heavy-handed public management: it gives corporations incentives to pursue satisfactory service and stable profits rather than short-sighted large gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual appropriation for genuine natural monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a monopoly or semi-monopoly survives and becomes in effect a "natural" monopoly, the state should adopt a policy of gradually appropriating for the benefit of the community the substantial economic advantages which these corporations have acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation is presented as a long-term, generational process rather than abrupt expropriation; it follows prolonged testing of corporations' fitness as national economic agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit municipal franchise terms and retain right of purchase
rubrics_metrics.description: Public service corporations' franchises should be restricted to limited terms and municipalities should retain a right of purchase; privileges that increase automatically in value with city growth should not be permanently alienated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy emphasis is on converting permanent private franchises into temporary tenancies so that increases in value accrue to the community; leases should be stringently arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor mixed municipal ownership with private operation until public administration improves
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed system of public ownership and private operation generally offers the better chance of satisfactory results while municipal civil service remains disorganized and inefficient; mixed systems must sharply distinguish responsibilities of public and private agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal operation has theoretical advantages, but practical performance of civil service matters; avoid divided and confused personal responsibility by creating clear role distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal policy must finance permanent improvements and provide for debt extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipality guaranteeing monopolies and leasing enjoyment thereof should make permanent improvements at its own expense; its financial organization must allow borrowing sufficient for construction and debt extinction; leases must cover interest and principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cities adopting leasing policies must adapt borrowing limits and fiscal methods; failure to provide finance undermines the policy and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use aggressive legal, fiscal, and competitive measures to reclaim intolerable permanent monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where private companies enjoy complete or substantial permanent monopolies, "persistent and ruthless war" should be declared: nullify permanent franchises by legal means, tax heavily, establish competitive services where feasible, and pressure companies to exchange permanent possession for limited tenancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames such measures as justified to reclaim essential communal resources; actions should remain "under the law" though vigorous — measures that would otherwise be unfair may be used deliberately to bring monopolies to terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal appropriation of monopoly-enabling railroad assets
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal government should take possession of railroad property represented by terminals, permanent rights of way, tracks, and stations — the property that enables railroads to become monopolies — to secure the community's share of increasing value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals range from slow gradual appropriation (in return for government credit) to immediate purchase and conversion of railroad securities into government securities, followed by leasing to private corporations for defined terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect existing property values and delegate clear economic authority in reorganizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any reorganization of railroads or other corporations should carefully respect existing railroad and property values unless management obstinately refuses concessions; where private agencies are used their delegated power should be complete within defined limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorganizations must aim to keep benefits of existing private organization and avoid half-measures that confuse responsibility; if private agents cannot be trusted, dispense with them entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat industrial corporations case-by-case according to industry conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial corporations cannot be uniformly treated; each industry should be considered in relation to special conditions — where combination tends to natural monopoly (control of mineral/land/water rights) public ownership and private operation may be required; where not, measures of expediency vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No general rule fits all industries; apply recognition, regulation, and graduated taxation as experimental, industry-specific measures until suitability is demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt graduated inheritance tax to mitigate existing wealth inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigation of existing inequalities can be achieved without injustice by a graduated inheritance tax; preserving fortunes intact over a certain amount is not desirable in public or individual interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: large fortunes neither benefit owners nor the public; state should assume public duties of using wealth for social good rather than relying on accidental philanthropy. The tax is presented as an accepted principle in some states and abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community should appropriate value increases created by social activity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no injustice in appropriating for the community those increases in value which are due merely to a general increase in population and business; semi-monopolistic organization enables separation of social from individual product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle supports taxing or otherwise recapturing value that arises from communal growth rather than individual enterprise; the aim is to secure community share of socially-created value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept temporary individual losses and reduced prosperity for long-term national economic balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A reorganization to secure a healthier distribution of wealth will cause individual loss, suffering, and temporary reduced prosperity, but such wounds are worth the penalty if they serve the national economic interest and produce a more wholesome distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should weigh trade-offs candidly: industrial efficiency need not be compromised because of redistributed fruits; distinction is made between industrial efficiency and short-term business prosperity.
